---
title: "Batches of conditions"
---

`solveODEBatch()` solves $K$ conditions of one model in a single
`.Call`, in three phases. The main thread reads the arguments of
every condition from R into plain C++ structures. OpenMP threads then
run the $K$ solves with dynamic scheduling, so a slow condition does
not hold up the others; the workers touch neither the R API nor R's
allocator, which is not thread-safe. The main thread finally builds the
result list. When `times` fixes the output grid, the result
arrays are allocated before the parallel phase and the workers write
into them directly; a root event leaves the row count open until the
solve ends, and its output is copied afterwards.

Each condition is solved as `solveODE()` would solve it: the
workers share no state and form no reductions across conditions, so the
result is bitwise identical to the serial loop, whatever the thread
count and schedule.

The thread count is the request, at most the number of processors, also
for fewer conditions than threads, so that OpenMP keeps the threads of its
team from one call to the next; `attr(, "threads")` of the result reports
it. It is one for a single condition, and it falls to one
inside an enclosing OpenMP region, where the caller already runs in
parallel, and in a child created by `fork()`, because the OpenMP
thread pool does not survive a fork; a `pthread_atfork` handler
marks the child. The BLAS library's own threads are set to one for the
duration of a batch and restored afterwards. A second
`pthread_atfork` handler, installed once per process, sets the
BLAS and OpenMP thread counts to one across every `fork()` and
restores them in the parent. `forkGuard()` reports which
BLAS library was found, and `batchAvailable()` whether a model
runs its conditions in parallel.

`prepareBatch()` performs the first phase once and keeps the
converted arguments in a handle; `solveBatch()` then solves the
same conditions with new parameter values, tangents, Hessians,
cotangents, curvatures, adjoint controls or stores of unchanged shapes,
as an optimiser does at every iteration; new tolerances need a new
`prepareBatch()`. Reverse-mode solves use the same entry with one cotangent
per condition, and `cvode()` models provide the same batch
entry.
